passage: Wednesday, 9 pm. Three evenings on the Trigonometry chapter and I still cannot solve the heights and distances questions. Today I added it up: many hours for a small share of marks, while other units are half done. I told Parul Ma'am after class. I thought she would say try harder. Instead she pulled out the marks list and said, "Let us make sure the pass is safe first. Do the units you can finish, then come back to Trigonometry if time is left." It felt like quitting for about a minute and then like relief. I made a new list: Units 1, 2 and 4 first. Trigonometry goes on the last page with a question mark. Early sleep tonight. Eshaan

subtype: Approach: cutting losses on one weak unit [Revision]
passage: In the kasba's only higher secondary school, Siddharth had spent two weeks of evenings on three-dimensional geometry and still couldn't picture a single plane. The Maths pre-board was a month away, and his last score was 26 out of 80, just short of a pass. On Monday he stayed back, eyes red, and showed Anand Sir his notebook, full of crossed-out attempts. Anand Sir turned to the marks scheme. "This chapter is six marks. Matrices, calculus and probability together are more than forty, and you already half know them." Siddharth frowned. "So I just skip it?" "For now. Make the pass safe first. If there's a week left at the end, come back to it, and I'll help." Siddharth crossed out 3D in his plan and wrote "later, maybe". For the first time in weeks, his shoulders dropped.

qa.q: How many marks is the 3D geometry chapter worth?
What does Siddharth's frown when he asks about skipping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt uneasy and doubtful, as if dropping the chapter might be quitting.

qa.q: What makes this a sensible trade for Siddharth?
qa.a: The six-mark chapter was eating his evenings, while matrices, calculus and probability offer more than forty marks he half knows, so securing those first makes the pass safer.

qa.q: How might Anand Sir see Siddharth's red eyes and crossed-out notebook?
qa.a: He likely sees a student working hard in the wrong place, and wants to redirect that effort rather than pile on more hours.

grounding: Shows a student and teacher agreeing to secure the pass through other units first and return to a costly hard chapter only if time remains.
